transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Schiavone.
President Trump is praising NVIDIA's decision to reinstate Jensen Wong as the company's
CEO, even after Wong was linked to a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and PR's Danielle
Kurtzleben has more.
In a social media post, Trump wrote that Wong should lead the company "in order to ensure
the success and prosperity of not only the company but the American economy."
He added that the U.S. government "has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to
NVIDIA poses any risk to national security."
In announcing the reinstatement, NVIDIA said that they had "received input from senior
levels of the United States government, helping them conclude that Wong was not a security
risk."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio drafted a memo earlier this year, warning that Wong was in
a relationship with a woman whom U.S. intelligence services believed to have ties to a Chinese
spy agency.
Danielle Kurtzleben, NPR News, The White House.
A federal appeals court has revived President Trump's bid to move his hush money case from
state to federal court.
The decision keeps the door open to the president's efforts to erase his criminal conviction,
and PR's Ryan Lucas reports.
A jury in New York State found Trump guilty in 2024 of falsifying business records to hide
hush money payments made to adult film star Stormy Daniels.
Trump has fought his criminal conviction, arguing in part that the case should be moved
from state court to federal court, where he could argue presidential immunity.
Now a three-judge panel on the Second Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled that a district
court judge had aired in his decision that Trump's state case categorically couldn't
be moved to federal court after his conviction.
The appeals court sent the matter back to the district court to consider Trump's removal
request again.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
An Israeli medical charity says the expansion of Israeli military checkpoints in the occupied
West Bank is risking lives by preventing Palestinian ambulances from reaching patients at hospitals,
and PR's Lauren Freyer reports from Tel Aviv.
Physicians for Human Rights Israel has published interviews with 25 Palestinian paramedics,
including one who says Israeli soldiers prevented him from reaching a wounded man nearby, leaving
him to bleed to death.
In a new report, the group cites a 350 percent spike in such incidents, including violence
directed at medical workers themselves between 2022 and 2024.
Imran Ennati, the report's author, calls this collective punishment.
By blocking an ambulance to evacuate a patient, you're blocking the health care to the whole
Palestinian community.
Asked about the report, the Israeli military told NPR it works to facilitate safe passage
of medical teams subject to security assessment.
Lauren Freyer, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
On Wall Street, the Dow gained 1,447 points, closing at 49,595.
The S&P picked up 326.
This is NPR.
Honda is recalling almost a million vehicles due to safety concerns about Takata airbags,
which can rupture when exposed to high humidity.
These include several 2012-2013 models, including Acuras, CRVs, Civics, and Accords.
Delta Airlines passengers are still experiencing travel disruptions following an automation
system problem, bad timing for Thanksgiving holiday travelers.
Marlon Hyde from member station WABE has details.
Inside Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, Delta Airlines' primary hub, travelers
have seen dozens of canceled flights, and over 250 were delayed, according to FlightAware.
Maliki Forna just arrived in Atlanta after an almost four-hour delay.
He, his wife, and three kids were rebooked while traveling from New York to South Carolina.
We were going to get in at 11, and instead we're getting in now, further away.
So it's a little bit inconvenient, but we're coming to visit families, so we're happy that
we're going to be able to see them.
Delta set in a statement that operations are stable today, with automation systems fully
restored.
For NPR News, I'm Marlon Hyde in Atlanta.
A federal appeals court says it's okay for the Army to detonate several tons of degraded
bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant.
President Trump had ordered the Army to wait for a court decision.
Sixty-eight barrels of leaded materials are involved, and environmental activists objected
to the introduction of the materials into the atmosphere.
The Army has said there's a risk cold weather will further destabilize the materials.
I'm Louise Schiavone, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: NVIDIA reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO; Trump praises move despite alleged Chinese spy link
Federal appeals court revives Trump's bid to move hush money conviction to federal court
Israeli medical charity says West Bank checkpoints are blocking Palestinian ambulances, risking lives
Dow gains 1,447 points to close at 49,595 on Wall Street
Honda recalls nearly a million vehicles over Takata airbags that can rupture in humidity
Delta Airlines cancels dozens of Atlanta flights after automation system problem during Thanksgiving travel
Federal appeals court allows Army to detonate degraded bomb-making materials at Iowa ammunition plant
